title: Gardens with running water
hookLine: four-part gardens with water channels, reflecting the gardens of the Qur'an

cards: "Gardens underneath which rivers flow." That's a phrase from the Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation, describing what waits for those who believe and do good.

Now step through a gate into a walled courtyard in Isfahan, or Granada, or Agra. Stone paths cross in the middle. Along each runs a narrow channel of water, so shallow it barely moves, holding a strip of sky.
Where the channels meet, there's a pool, or a fountain murmuring. Trees, shade, the smell of wet stone. Today: gardens with running water.

teach.b: The Qur'an's word for paradise, jannah, is the ordinary Arabic word for a garden. So when the Qur'an describes the life to come, it describes shade, fruit and water.

teach.h: RIVERS OF WATER, MILK, WINE, HONEY.
teach.b: One passage, in surah forty-seven, even names its rivers: rivers of water that never goes stale, of milk, of wine, of honey.
Garden builders worked with a plan often called by a Persian name, chahar bagh, four gardens: a walled rectangle split by water channels into four parts that meet at a center.

Some readers link those channels to the rivers of surah forty-seven. Others point out that walled Persian gardens are older than Islam, and say Muslims took up the old plan and gave it new meaning. Both can be true.
Either way, think what water meant to the builders. Isfahan, Agra and Granada are hot in summer. Water you could hear was wealth.
Water you could see moving was life. A garden with running water was a small earthly reminder of a promise, built by hand, to be walked in.

And these gardens were made for sitting, not racing through: sitting beside a channel in the shade, and listening. Some were planted around tombs, so the dead rested inside a picture of the garden they hoped for.
In the Qur'an the garden is a promise. The garden on earth kept that promise in view.

how: Visitors still walk the channel gardens of places such as the Alhambra's Generalife, Isfahan and the Taj Mahal, and some Muslim homes keep courtyard gardens with a fountain or pool at the center.

games.why: the gardens ran water in narrow channels beside the paths, meeting at a pool or fountain: water you could see, hear and sit beside.

practice: Sit near water or a plant, a glass on the table, a tap running into a bowl, a houseplant, a tree outside, and look at it as the center of a garden, where all the paths meet.
Listen to the water or watch the light on it; with a plant, choose one leaf and take in its edge, its color, the way it turns toward the light.
If you pray, you can say al-hamdu lillah, praise be to God, for water; if you don't, just stay with it.

wordCard.voice: Jannah. The Qur'an's word for paradise and garden, pictured as gardens under which rivers flow, and echoed in walled courtyards split by channels. Today's word.
